stem: You change the AWS provider constraint from `~> 6.0` to `~> 6.66` and run `terraform init`. Terraform exits with an error saying the locked version does not match the new constraint. What is the correct next step?
options: Edit the lock file by hand to match the new constraint, then rerun `terraform init`.
Run `terraform init -upgrade` so Terraform selects the newest version allowed by the new constraint.
Run `terraform apply -upgrade` to update the provider during the next deployment.
objective: Change a provider version constraint and re-run terraform init with appropriate flags to update the lock file

stem: After running `terraform init -upgrade` with constraint `~> 6.66`, you restore the constraint to `~> 6.0` but run only `terraform init` (no flags). What happens to the lock file?
options: Terraform raises an error and refuses to initialise until you add `-reconfigure`.
Terraform rewrites the lock file to the latest 6.x release automatically.
Terraform deletes the lock file and forces you to rerun with `-upgrade`.
Terraform leaves the lock file unchanged because it does not re-select already-installed providers without `-upgrade`.
objective: Change a provider version constraint and re-run terraform init with appropriate flags to update the lock file

stem: A colleague asks whether running `terraform init -upgrade` on a production configuration is dangerous because it might overwrite state. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes — `-upgrade` rewrites both the lock file and the state file, so you should back up state first.
Yes — any `terraform init` run can destroy resources if a provider version changes behaviour.
No — `terraform init` never deletes your existing configuration or state, regardless of flags; it only updates downloaded plugins and the lock file.
No — but only because `-upgrade` skips state entirely and only affects module source code.
objective: Change a provider version constraint and re-run terraform init with appropriate flags to update the lock file
